passages.original: Videte tamen, obsecro, quale sit ideo uolenti et currenti misericordiam dei non necessariam, quae illum etiam praeuenit, ut curreret. quia de quodam ait apostolus: quod uult faciat, ibi, ut arbitror, ubi sequitur et dicit: non peccat, nubat — quasi pro magno habendum sit uelle nubere, ubi de adiutorio diuinae misericordiae operosius disputatur, aut uero etiam ibi prodest aliquid uelle, nisi deus prouidentia, qua gubernat omnia, marem feminamque coniungat — aut quoniam ad Philemonem scripsit apostolus: ut non quasi ex necessitate bonum eius esset, sed uoluntarium, quasi aliter sit uoluntarium bonum, nisi cum deus operatur in nobis et uelle et operari pro bona uoluntate; aut quia in Deuteronomio scriptum est: uitam et mortem dedit ante faciem hominis, bonum et malum et ammonuit ut eligeret uitam, quasi et ipsa ammonitio non de misericordia ueniat, uel aliquid prodesset eligere uitam, nisi deus eligendi caritatem inspiraret et electam habere praestaret, de quo dictum est: quoniam ira in indignatione eius et uita in uoluntate eius;
passages.english: Yet see, I beg you, what sort of [argument] it is that the mercy of God is therefore not necessary to one who wills and runs, [a mercy] which even went before him so that he might run: because the apostle says of a certain man, "let him do what he will", in the place, I think, where he goes on to say, "he does not sin, let him marry" (as if wanting to marry were to be regarded as a great thing, when the help of divine mercy is being discussed at such length; or indeed as if even there willing were of any use unless God, by the providence with which he governs all things, joins male and female together); or because the apostle wrote to Philemon, "so that his good might not be as if from necessity, but voluntary", as if a good were voluntary in any other way than when God works in us both to will and to work for [his] good will; or because it is written in Deuteronomy, "he set life and death before the face of man, good and evil", and admonished him to choose life, as if the admonition itself did not also come from mercy, or as if choosing life would be of any use unless God inspired the love of choosing [it] and granted [him] to hold [it] once chosen, of whom it was said, "for wrath is in his indignation, and life in his will";
passages.notes: The opening clause (quale sit ideo ... non necessariam) is elliptical; it seems to report an opponent's inference that God's mercy is not needed by one who wills and runs, and the translation supplies "[argument]". The quotations are from 1 Corinthians 7:36, Philemon 14, Philippians 2:13, Deuteronomy 30:15–19 and Psalm 30(29):5 (Latin version).
